newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland blazed trail for Russian rouble reform.
newsitem.headline: Poland blazed trail for Russian rouble reform.

text.p: Russia's planned rouble reform follows a trail blazed by Poland, which dropped four zeroes from its inflation-ravaged zloty on January 1, 1995, but the project got mixed reviews in Warsaw.
A Warsaw central bank official told Reuters the Russian move, announced by President Boris Yeltsin on Monday, could have similar positive results to those in Poland.

"In Russia, with falling inflation and growing foreign reserves, the redenomination should result in more confidence in the rouble, as it did (for the zloty) in Poland," said Jacek Osinski, deputy head of the National Bank of Poland monetary policy department.
Yeltsin announced that from January 1, 1998, Russia would redenominate its currency, cutting off three zeroes, and introducing a new rouble worth 1,000 roubles (17 cents).
Russia will allow only one year in which both old and new money are used at the same time, unlike Poland which pulled the last old notes from circulation last December after two years.
Many of the reasons for the Russian change, and public anxieties associated with it, are common to both countries.

In Poland, the so-called "denominacja" turned 10,000 old zlotys into one new zloty (28 cents). The decision came once inflation that had turned even poor people into zloty millionaires was judged sufficiently low for the effects to be lasting.

Some Polish commentators, including former finance minister Jerzy Osiatynski, argued that Russia's decision to redenominate next year might be premature as, unlike Poland, it had not first tackled major economic restructuring.
"This will be a very risky operation," Osiatynski, now in opposition, told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily, adding that it should delay it at least a year and preferably two or three.
He said Russia had not achieved macroeconomic stability, was vulnerable to pressure from loss-making sectors like steel and mining and had yet to fully tackle mass privatisation.
"I don't know if Russia's banking system will be able to cope with such an operation," he said, adding that Russian society also did not have confidence in the authorities.
Cezary Jozefiak, head of Warsaw's conservative Adam Smith Centre economic thinktank, told the daily that if Russia redenominated now it would have to repeat the process later.
As in Russia, the Polish redonomination aroused various anxieties. Some economists questioned whether, with inflation well above 20 percent, it was not too soon.
Many Poles, bitterly remembering their losses from past communist-era tinkering with the currency, were apprehensive.
Some feared shops would use the chance to round up prices, although shopkeepers had to quote prices in old and new zlotys.
But the experience proved smoother than many feared, especially after adverts featuring a spoof gangster movie and a cuddly cartoon hamster helped people understand the change.

The redenomination was a major step toward boosting confidence in the currency after frightening price rises during the dismantling of the communist system in 1989 and 1990, when people rushed to spend money before it lost value.
"In retrospect, I can't see anything we could have done much better," said Zbigniew Marski, advisor to Poland's central bank president, who sat on the committee overseeing the change.

"We did it...in 1995 because it was the fifth year of falling inflation, at the end of 1994 it was already below 30 percent (29.5 percent)," he said, adding that the falling inflation trend proved to be sustainable.

Consumer prices fell by as much as eight percentage points in 1995 and declined further in 1996 to reach an annualized inflation rate of 18.5 percent in December last year and 15.3 percent in June this year.
($ = 5802 Russian Roubles)
($ = 3.462 Polish Zlotys)
